title: The Producers
full_review:
It's not often that a successful movie becomes an even more successful stage musical and then makes it back to the silver screen.

But "The Producers" (Universal/Columbia) is that rare exception, and it turns out to be a first-rate filming of Mel Brooks' Broadway megahit. (The show's still running strong in New York and London, but now everyone can see it with most of the legendary cast intact.)

Max Bialystock (Nathan Lane) is a losing-streak producer with a string of flops to his credit, the latest being "Funny Boy," a musical version of "Hamlet."

When nerdy, stage-struck accountant Leo Bloom (Matthew Broderick) -- a high-strung bean counter with a blue security blanket -- comes to do Max's books, he casually remarks that one could actually make more money with a flop than with a hit. Max hatches a scheme to do just that: bankroll a show that's doomed to failure and retire to Rio with the investment. (It should be noted that Max gets his money from rich old ladies with whom he role-plays amorous scenarios, but this is dramatized with a light comic touch.)

After poring over various scripts, they pick the worst possible one, "Springtime for Hitler," an adulatory musical about Adolf Hitler, and get the rights from an eccentric Nazi, Franz Liebkind (Will Ferrell), whom they visit on his Manhattan rooftop, where he tends his carrier pigeons. (He sends the birds to Argentina with messages for Der Fuhrer.)

In short order, they engage flamboyant director Roger DeBris (Gary Beach) and his even more outrageous aide-de-camp, Carmen Ghia (Roger Bart), to helm the show. They hire as their secretary a sweet-natured Swedish bombshell, Ulla (Uma Thurman), who shows up at their doorstop to audition, and promise her a part in the show later on.

Disaster is assured, or is it?

Director Susan Stroman makes an auspicious film debut, faithfully re-creating her acclaimed staging, but opening it up for the stage in the manner of 1950s screen musicals, so that the result honors its theatrical traditions -- some characters address the camera, for instance -- while imaginatively enhancing it in cinematic terms.

The "Little Old Lady" ballet conceived as a fantasy on stage now takes place in Central Park, as the elderly biddies (Andrea Martin and Debra Monk among them) come out of their expensive Fifth Avenue apartment buildings on their walkers.

Mel Brooks' tuneful songs are satisfyingly performed, with none of the choppy editing
that was so disconcerting in the film version of "Chicago," and unlike that film, dancers are filmed from head to toe. The orchestra has a satisfyingly lush sound, and the lip-syncing is first-rate, just like the old days at MGM.

Stage alumni Lane, Broderick, Beach and Bart are all in predictably top form, and are joined by an extremely funny Ferrell and a surprisingly good Thurman (who proves a more than credible singer and dancer).

Like the Mel Brooks film with Zero Mostel and Gene Wilder of almost 40 years ago, much of the humor is intentionally off-color. A Catholic Film Office review of the 1967 original praised the cast, albeit with a warning that the film was only for those who "don't mind bawdy and blatant satire."

Given familiarity with the show, and now-classic status of the 1967 film, the subversiveness of the original has been softened with time. We now take for granted the politically incorrect, if tongue-in-cheek, concept. Be warned there is some off-color dialogue, and DeBris and Ghia are beyond camp in their outrageous effeminate mannerisms, but it's all fairly innocuous.

This is still adult fare -- though perhaps acceptable for older adolescents -- but it's hard not to smile at Mel Brooks' (and co-scriptwriter Thomas Meehan's) inspired lunacy, and Stroman's unbeatable Broadway pizzazz. And the price of movie ticket sure beats Broadway!

The film contains some bawdy and outrageous humor including gay stereotypes, cross-dressing, sexual innuendo, suggestive costuming and dancing, some crude language and comic violence. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
